questions.question: Why is common residence not the sole defining feature of a joint family?
questions.solution_html:
• A joint family is defined by continuing relationships, rights and obligations among relatives
  • rather than residence alone.
  •  Members may share property, financial responsibilities, ritual duties and mutual
  • support.
  •  Members living separately because of employment or education may continue to
  • function as part of the joint family.
  •  Conversely, people sharing a house do not necessarily constitute a joint family unless
  • such kinship obligations exist.
  • Marking: Shared obligations, continuity despite separate residence, and distinction between
  • household and family — (1 mark) each.
  • Family: Equal access to education, shared domestic responsibilities and participation
  • in decisions challenge gender discrimination.
  • Equal citizenship: Equal rights and protection against discrimination build security
  • and belonging.
  • Greater decision-making power: Education and independent earnings can increase
  • women’s influence over marriage, household expenditure, childbirth and children’s
  • education.
  • Changes in landownership and agriculture: Land reforms, commercial farming and
  • new sources of wealth can alter the influence of traditional landlords.
  • Religious and philosophical texts: The Vedas, Upanishads and Dharmashastras reveal
  • ideas about social duties, hierarchy and moral order.
  • Economic: Industrialisation, technological development, market expansion and
  • occupational diversification.
  • 17(b). Analyse how endogamy reproduces caste as a closed social group across
  • generations.
  • Endogamy means marriage within a defined social group. Caste endogamy restricts marriage
  • to members of the same caste or recognised subgroup, thereby maintaining caste
  • boundaries.
  • Control of membership: Restricting marriage limits the formation of family relationships
  • across castes. Children are generally assigned a caste identity through descent, allowing
  • membership to continue across generations.
  • Transmission of resources: Marriage within caste helps circulate property, wealth and social
  • connections within established networks.
  • Preservation of hierarchy: Families may treat marriage as a means of maintaining caste
  • status, preventing unions that challenge inherited distinctions.
  • Socialisation: Children learn caste preferences through family expectations, marriage
  • practices, community networks and everyday discussion.
  • Regulation of sexuality: Control over women’s partner choices and sexuality plays a
  • particularly important role in maintaining caste boundaries.
  • Sanctions: Inter-caste couples may face emotional pressure, exclusion, withdrawal of
  • support or violence. Such sanctions discourage boundary-crossing.
  • Modern reproduction: Matrimonial websites, professional networks and educated families
  • may continue caste-based partner selection, showing that modernisation does not
  • automatically end endogamy.
  • Endogamy consequently connects marriage, descent, property and social control. It is a
  • central mechanism through which caste persists despite changes in occupation and public
  • interaction.
  • Suggested marking: Definition — 1; mechanisms — 6; conclusion — 1.
  • 18(a). Describe the meaning of caste and explain its major characteristics.
  • Caste is a system of hereditary social stratification in which groups are differentiated by
  • birth, marriage rules, status and historically associated occupations. In everyday life, caste
  • generally refers to jati; the fourfold varna scheme is a broader classificatory model.
  • Major characteristics
  • Birth-based membership: Individuals ordinarily acquire caste membership through
  • birth.

questions.question: Examine the reasons why the experiences of marginalised groups are central to the subaltern perspective.
questions.solution_html:
• The subaltern perspective studies society from the standpoint of groups subordinated by
  • caste, class, gender or other power relations.
  •  Elite accounts often overlook the experiences of peasants, workers, Dalits, Adivasis
  • and women.
  •  Their experiences reveal how domination operates in everyday life.
  •  Their voices also demonstrate agency through resistance, negotiation and collective
  • action.
  • Example: Studying a peasant struggle through participants’ accounts rather than only official
  • records.
  • Educational institutions: Inclusive teaching, equal opportunities and effective
  • responses to harassment support gender equality.
  • Dialogue and cooperation: Interaction through neighbourhood groups, schools and
  • workplaces reduces prejudice and builds trust.
  • Changes in gender roles: Employment can encourage the sharing of domestic work
  • and childcare and challenge the assumption that men alone should earn.
  • However, women may experience a double burden when paid work increases without a
  • corresponding redistribution of household responsibilities.
  • Marking: Two explained changes — 1½ marks each.
  • Democratic politics: Elections, Panchayati Raj and representation of disadvantaged
  • groups create new opportunities for leadership.
  • Epics and literary works: The Ramayana, Mahabharata and other literature provide
  • representations of kinship, gender, kingship and social values.
  • Political: Growth of democratic participation, citizenship, bureaucratic administration
  • and legal-rational authority.
  • Segmental division: Society is divided into groups with their own identities, customs
  • and social networks.

questions.question: Examine communalism as a process that turns religious difference into social or political antagonism.
questions.solution_html:
• Examine communalism as a process that turns religious difference into social or political
  • antagonism.
  • Communalism develops when religious communities are presented as groups with uniform
  • and opposing interests.
  •  Religious identities become boundaries separating “us” from “them.”
  •  Political mobilisation, stereotypes and selective accounts of history portray another
  • community as a threat.
  •  This can produce discrimination, segregation, hostility and violence.
  • Religious diversity itself does not necessarily produce communalism; antagonism is socially
  • and politically constructed.
  • Workplaces: Equal pay, fair recruitment, promotion opportunities and protection
  • against harassment promote dignity and participation.
  • Marking: (1 mark) for each institution with an appropriate explanation.
  • Respect for cultural diversity: Recognition of different languages, religions and
  • customs allows people to preserve their identities while participating in shared social
  • life.
  • Education and non-farm employment: Migration, salaried work and access to
  • information can reduce dependence on dominant landowning groups.
  • Inscriptions and historical records: Inscriptions, genealogies and chronicles offer
  • evidence about land grants, political authority, religious patronage and social groups.
  • These sources require critical interpretation because prescribed ideals may differ from
  • everyday practices.
  • Social and cultural: Expansion of education, scientific thinking, individual choice and
  • challenges to inherited status.
  • Modernisation is uneven and does not automatically eliminate inequality.
  • Hierarchy: Castes are placed in unequal status relationships, although rankings can
  • vary and be contested.

questions.question: Analyse how the structural-functional perspective views institutions as interconnected social relations.
questions.solution_html:
• social relations?
  • The structural-functional perspective views society as a system of interdependent
  • institutions.
  •  Institutions such as family, economy, education and religion consist of organised
  • roles, norms and relationships.
  •  Each contributes to social continuity through functions such as socialisation
  • production and regulation.
  •  A change in one institution affects others.
  • Example: Expansion of education changes employment opportunities, marriage
  • expectations and family relations.
  • Purity and pollution: These ideas have historically justified status differences and
  • practices of exclusion.

questions.question: Describe any three factors that influence changing rural power.
questions.solution_html:
• Unequal privileges and disabilities: Access to land, education, religious spaces and
  • authority has been unequally distributed.
  • These characteristics have changed substantially. Caste continues through a combination of
  • marriage patterns, social networks, inequalities and political identities rather than through
  • an entirely unchanged traditional order.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning and jati–varna distinction — 2; characteristics — 5;
  • contemporary qualification — 1.
  • 18(b). Describe the risks of digitalisation, including misinformation, surveillance, privacy
  • and the reproduction of inequality.
  • Digitalisation involves the growing use of digital technologies in communication, work
  • education, governance and everyday life. Alongside its benefits, it produces significant social
  • risks.
  • Misinformation: False or misleading content can circulate rapidly through social media and
  • messaging platforms. It can damage reputations, intensify prejudice and encourage poorly
  • informed decisions. Disinformation refers more specifically to deliberately deceptive
  • content.
  • Surveillance: Governments, companies and other actors can monitor activities through
  • location records, online behaviour, cameras and databases. Excessive monitoring can restrict
  • autonomy and discourage participation or dissent.
  • Privacy risks: Large-scale collection and sharing of personal data can expose individuals to
  • profiling, identity theft, fraud and unwanted disclosure. Consent may be weakened when
  • users cannot understand or meaningfully refuse data practices.
  • Digital inequality: Differences in internet access, devices, affordability and skills affect
  • participation in education, employment and public services. Gender, class, caste, disability
  • age and location can shape these differences.
  • Reproduction of discrimination: Algorithms trained on unequal or biased data can
  • reproduce disadvantage in recruitment, lending and other decisions.
  • Exclusion from services: Digital-only systems can disadvantage people who lack connectivity
  • documentation, language support or technical assistance.
  • Example: An online application process may expand convenience while excluding applicants
  • without reliable internet or digital literacy.
  • Addressing these risks requires accessible systems, digital literacy, privacy safeguards
  • accountable institutions and meaningful alternatives for people facing digital exclusion.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; four specified risks — 6; example/conclusion — 1.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) . Describe the risks of digitalisation, including misinformation, surveillance, privacy

questions.question: Examine the ways in which factors other than income shape class position.
questions.solution_html:
•  Wealth and property: Land, housing and inherited assets provide security and
  • advantages beyond current earnings.
  •  Occupation and education: Job security, qualifications, skills and authority affect life
  • chances.
  •  Social background and networks: Caste, gender, family connections and access to
  • influential people shape opportunities and mobility.
  • Thus, two people with similar incomes may occupy different class positions because their
  • assets, security and opportunities differ.

questions.question: Describe the central present-day debate about change and equality in the caste system.
questions.solution_html:
• system.
  • The central debate concerns whether modernisation and democratic change are weakening
  • caste or transforming the ways it operates.
  •  Education, urbanisation, occupational mobility and legal equality have challenged
  • hereditary restrictions.
  •  Yet discrimination, endogamy, unequal resources and caste-based exclusion
  • continue.
  •  Therefore, changes in caste practices do not necessarily indicate the achievement of
  • substantive equality.

questions.question: Examine the ways in which migration can reshape caste and class relations.
questions.solution_html:
•  Migration may weaken local caste controls by providing anonymity, new occupations
  • and interaction across caste boundaries.
  •  Earnings and remittances can improve class position and reduce dependence on local
  • landlords or employers.
  •  However, caste networks may continue to organise recruitment, housing and
  • marriage, while insecure employment may reproduce disadvantage.
  • Migration can therefore create mobility while also carrying existing inequalities into new
  • settings.
  • Answer one question from each pair. Each carries (8 marks).
  • 14(a). Explain the meaning and key dimensions of agrarian change in India.
  • Agrarian change refers to transformations in agriculture and in the social relationships
  • organised around land, labour and agricultural production. It includes changes in ownership
  • technology, markets, class relations and rural power.
  • Landownership and tenure: Land reforms sought to abolish intermediaries, regulate
  • tenancy and redistribute surplus land. Their effects varied across regions. Unequal
  • ownership, insecure tenancy and fragmentation remain significant features of agrarian
  • society.
  • Technology and production: Irrigation, improved seeds, fertilisers and mechanisation
  • increased agricultural productivity in many areas. The Green Revolution particularly
  • benefited regions and cultivators with access to land, water and capital, contributing to
  • uneven development.
  • Commercialisation: Cultivation increasingly responds to markets through cash crops
  • purchased inputs, credit and commercial supply chains. This creates opportunities but also
  • exposes cultivators to fluctuating prices, rising costs and indebtedness.
  • Labour relations: Hereditary service relationships and personal dependence have weakened
  • in many areas. Wage labour, seasonal migration and mechanisation have altered agricultural
  • employment, although caste and gender inequalities persist.
  • Class and power relations: Changes in land, credit and production have strengthened some
  • prosperous cultivators and rural entrepreneurs. Small farmers and landless workers often
  • face greater insecurity.
  • Diversification and migration: Rural households increasingly combine farming with
  • construction work, services, small businesses and migration.
  • Gender and ecology: Women undertake substantial agricultural work but often lack
  • ownership and decision-making power. Water scarcity, soil degradation and climate
  • variability also shape agrarian livelihoods.
  • Agrarian change is therefore an uneven transformation of rural production, inequality and
  • power.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; explained dimensions — 6; conclusion/example — 1.
  • 14(b). Analyse Ghurye’s treatment of tribes and integration, including criticisms of his
  • assimilationist approach.
  • G. S. Ghurye understood many Indian tribal communities through their historical interaction
  • with the wider Hindu social order. He challenged the idea that tribes were entirely isolated
  • societies.
  • Tribe–caste connections: Ghurye emphasised cultural contact and similarities between tribal
  • populations and surrounding Hindu communities. He described many tribes as “backward
  • Hindus,” reflecting his interpretation that they had varying degrees of incorporation into
  • Hindu society.
  • Opposition to isolation: He opposed policies that would preserve tribal communities in
  • isolation. He favoured their participation in wider economic, educational and political life.
  • Assimilation: His approach generally supported incorporation into the wider Hindu social
  • order and national society. Education, communication and economic development were
  • important means of overcoming marginalisation.
  • Criticisms
  •  Cultural diversity: The category “backward Hindus” can obscure the distinct
  • religions, languages, institutions and identities of tribal communities.
  •  Hindu-centred interpretation: It treats incorporation into Hindu society as the
  • expected direction of change.
  •  Power and exploitation: Cultural incorporation does not necessarily remove
  • dispossession, indebtedness or exploitation.
  •  Autonomy and consent: Assimilation may neglect communities’ rights to determine
  • their own futures.
  •  Cultural loss: Incorporation can undermine indigenous knowledge and collective
  • institutions.
  • Ghurye’s contribution lies in highlighting historical connections between tribes and wider
  • society. However, an adequate approach to integration must combine equal opportunities
  • with cultural recognition, land rights and self-determination.
  • Suggested marking: Ghurye’s approach — 4; criticisms — 3; assessment — 1.
  • 15(a). Discuss discrimination, endogamy and unequal resources as contemporary
  • challenges related to caste.
  • Caste continues to shape opportunities and relationships despite substantial changes in
  • education, employment and public life.
  • Discrimination: Caste discrimination can occur in schools, workplaces, housing and public
  • spaces. It includes exclusion, humiliation, prejudiced judgments and unequal treatment.
  • Some forms are overt, while others operate through informal practices and networks.
  • Example: A qualified person may encounter housing exclusion because of their caste
  • identity.
  • Endogamy: Marriage within one’s caste remains a major mechanism of caste continuity.
  • Families may use caste-based networks and matrimonial preferences to regulate partner
  • selection. Opposition to inter-caste marriage can range from emotional pressure to violence.
  • Endogamy preserves caste boundaries by linking marriage with family status, inheritance
  • and community membership.
  • Unequal resources: Historical differences in landownership, education, assets and
  • occupational opportunities continue to influence present outcomes. Families with
  • substantial resources can provide better schooling, financial support and access to influential
  • networks. Disadvantaged households may face insecure work and limited opportunities for
  • accumulation.
  • Interconnection: Discrimination restricts opportunities, resource inequalities reduce
  • bargaining power, and endogamy helps transmit these advantages and disadvantages across
  • generations.
  • Addressing caste therefore requires both protection against exclusion and measures that
  • expand access to education, resources, dignified employment and freedom of marriage.
  • Suggested marking: Introduction — 1; three challenges — 6; conclusion — 1.
  • 15(b). Analyse why modern caste politics is not simply the survival of traditional politics.
  • Modern caste politics involves the transformation of caste identities through elections
  • democratic institutions, political parties and struggles over resources.
  • From inherited authority to electoral mobilisation: Traditional caste authority was closely
  • associated with hereditary status and local dominance. Electoral politics requires leaders to
  • mobilise voters and negotiate support.
  • Political participation of subordinated groups: Dalit, backward-caste and other movements
  • have challenged established hierarchies. Their mobilisation expresses demands for dignity
  • representation and redistribution.
  • New caste organisations: Caste associations may organise education, welfare, employment
  • support and political campaigns. These organisations use modern institutional forms and
  • communication technologies.
  • Coalition-building: Electoral success often requires alliances across castes. Political blocs are
  • constructed through negotiation rather than determined entirely by ritual hierarchy.
  • State resources and policy: Representation, reservations, welfare and access to public
  • institutions have become major political concerns. Caste thus becomes a basis for claims
  • upon the modern state.
  • Changing leadership: Education, organisational ability and political connections can create
  • leaders whose influence does not rest solely on traditional rank.
  • Continuing contradictions: Caste mobilisation can democratise power, but it can also
  • promote exclusion, elite capture and conflict.
  • Modern caste politics therefore combines inherited identities with new institutions and
  • aspirations. It may reproduce inequality, but it can also provide a means of challenging it.
  • Suggested marking: Central argument — 1; analysis — 6; balanced conclusion — 1.
  • 16(a). Examine changing inter-caste relations in work, politics and everyday interaction.
  • Inter-caste relations have changed through education, migration, democratic participation
  • economic development and anti-caste struggles. These changes vary across regions and
  • social settings.
  • Work: Hereditary links between caste and occupation have weakened in many sectors.
  • People from different castes work together in offices, factories, educational institutions and
  • service industries. However, caste networks still influence recruitment and advancement
  • while stigmatised work remains disproportionately associated with particular communities.
  • Politics: Electoral democracy has expanded participation and enabled historically
  • disadvantaged groups to challenge dominant castes. Political parties build inter-caste
  • alliances and negotiate competing demands. At the same time, caste competition can
  • generate polarisation and conflict.
  • Everyday interaction: Shared schools, transport, markets and workplaces have increased
  • contact across caste boundaries. Restrictions on commensality and physical interaction have
  • weakened in many settings.
  • Continuing boundaries: Greater interaction does not always produce intimate social
  • acceptance. Marriage remains strongly regulated by caste, and exclusion can persist in
  • housing, neighbourhood relations and access to common resources.
  • Uneven change: Urban anonymity and occupational diversity may weaken some controls
  • while local dependence and unequal landownership can sustain them elsewhere. Caste
  • discrimination also exists in cities.
  • Inter-caste relations thus show expanding cooperation alongside continuing hierarchy and
  • contested boundaries.
  • Suggested marking: Introduction — 1; work, politics and everyday interaction — 6; synthesis
  • — 1.
  • 16(b). Discuss the meaning and major dimensions of women’s empowerment.
  • Women’s empowerment is the process through which women gain resources, agency and
  • the ability to make meaningful decisions about their lives. It also involves transforming
  • institutions that sustain gender inequality.
  • Educational empowerment: Access to education, skills and digital literacy improves
  • knowledge, confidence and opportunities.
  • Economic empowerment: Access to decent employment, fair earnings, property, credit and
  • control over income strengthens independence and bargaining power.
  • Political empowerment: Voting, representation, leadership and participation in public
  • decisions enable women to influence policies and institutions.
  • Social empowerment: Freedom from restrictive norms, violence and discrimination
  • supports mobility, dignity and participation in community life.
  • Legal empowerment: Awareness of rights and effective access to justice help women
  • challenge unequal treatment and secure entitlements.
  • Health and bodily autonomy: Access to healthcare and the ability to make informed
  • decisions about marriage, sexuality and reproduction are essential.
  • Psychological empowerment: Self-confidence and recognition of one’s capacity to act help
  • women express preferences and challenge domination.
  • Example: A self-help group may offer savings and credit while also enabling collective action
  • and leadership.
  • Empowerment requires actual control and choice. Employment or formal representation
  • alone may have limited effects if others continue to control women’s decisions.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 2; explained dimensions — 5; example/conclusion — 1.
  • 17(a). Explain the structure and key characteristics of the Indian village community.
  • The Indian village community is a rural settlement whose members are connected through
  • residence, livelihoods, kinship, institutions and everyday interaction. Villages differ
  • considerably across regions.
  • Agrarian foundation: Agriculture and related activities have historically shaped village
  • livelihoods, social relations and seasonal routines.
  • Caste differentiation: Many villages contain several caste groups, sometimes living in distinct
  • neighbourhoods. Caste has influenced status, occupation and access to resources.
  • Class inequality: Differences between landowners, tenants, small cultivators and landless
  • workers create unequal economic positions.
  • Family and kinship: Families, lineages and marriage networks organise inheritance, support
  • and social obligations.
  • Local power: Landownership, caste position, wealth and political connections influence
  • leadership. Panchayats provide formal institutions of local governance.
  • Religious and cultural life: Festivals, religious institutions and local traditions can generate
  • shared participation, although participation may also reflect exclusion and hierarchy.
  • Cooperation and conflict: Villagers may cooperate in cultivation, ceremonies and local
  • development while also competing over land, wages, water and political authority.
  • External connections: Villages are linked to towns, markets, migration networks
  • government agencies and digital communication.
  • The village should therefore be understood as a changing and internally differentiated
  • community, rather than a uniformly harmonious or self-sufficient unit.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; structure and characteristics — 6; critical observation —

  • Respect for cultural diversity: Recognition of different languages, religions and
  • customs allows people to preserve their identities while participating in shared social
  • life.
  • Education and non-farm employment: Migration, salaried work and access to
  • information can reduce dependence on dominant landowning groups.
  • Inscriptions and historical records: Inscriptions, genealogies and chronicles offer
  • evidence about land grants, political authority, religious patronage and social groups.
  • These sources require critical interpretation because prescribed ideals may differ from
  • everyday practices.
  • Social and cultural: Expansion of education, scientific thinking, individual choice and
  • challenges to inherited status.
  • Modernisation is uneven and does not automatically eliminate inequality.
  • Hierarchy: Castes are placed in unequal status relationships, although rankings can
  • vary and be contested.

  • The structural-functional perspective views society as a system of interdependent

  •  A change in one institution affects others.

questions.question: Describe any three factors that influence changing rural power.
questions.solution_html:
• Unequal privileges and disabilities: Access to land, education, religious spaces and
  • authority has been unequally distributed.
  • These characteristics have changed substantially. Caste continues through a combination of
  • marriage patterns, social networks, inequalities and political identities rather than through
  • an entirely unchanged traditional order.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning and jati–varna distinction — 2; characteristics — 5;
  • contemporary qualification — 1.
  • 18(b). Describe the risks of digitalisation, including misinformation, surveillance, privacy
  • and the reproduction of inequality.
  • Digitalisation involves the growing use of digital technologies in communication, work
  • education, governance and everyday life. Alongside its benefits, it produces significant social
  • risks.
  • Misinformation: False or misleading content can circulate rapidly through social media and
  • messaging platforms. It can damage reputations, intensify prejudice and encourage poorly
  • informed decisions. Disinformation refers more specifically to deliberately deceptive
  • content.
  • Surveillance: Governments, companies and other actors can monitor activities through
  • location records, online behaviour, cameras and databases. Excessive monitoring can restrict
  • autonomy and discourage participation or dissent.
  • Privacy risks: Large-scale collection and sharing of personal data can expose individuals to
  • profiling, identity theft, fraud and unwanted disclosure. Consent may be weakened when
  • users cannot understand or meaningfully refuse data practices.
  • Digital inequality: Differences in internet access, devices, affordability and skills affect
  • participation in education, employment and public services. Gender, class, caste, disability
  • age and location can shape these differences.
  • Reproduction of discrimination: Algorithms trained on unequal or biased data can
  • reproduce disadvantage in recruitment, lending and other decisions.
  • Exclusion from services: Digital-only systems can disadvantage people who lack connectivity
  • documentation, language support or technical assistance.
  • Example: An online application process may expand convenience while excluding applicants
  • without reliable internet or digital literacy.
  • Addressing these risks requires accessible systems, digital literacy, privacy safeguards
  • accountable institutions and meaningful alternatives for people facing digital exclusion.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; four specified risks — 6; example/conclusion — 1.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) . Describe the risks of digitalisation, including misinformation, surveillance, privacy

questions.question: Examine the ways in which migration can reshape caste and class relations.
questions.solution_html:
•  Migration may weaken local caste controls by providing anonymity, new occupations
  • and interaction across caste boundaries.
  •  Earnings and remittances can improve class position and reduce dependence on local
  • landlords or employers.
  •  However, caste networks may continue to organise recruitment, housing and
  • marriage, while insecure employment may reproduce disadvantage.
  • Migration can therefore create mobility while also carrying existing inequalities into new
  • settings.
  • Answer one question from each pair. Each carries (8 marks).
  • 14(a). Explain the meaning and key dimensions of agrarian change in India.
  • Agrarian change refers to transformations in agriculture and in the social relationships
  • organised around land, labour and agricultural production. It includes changes in ownership
  • technology, markets, class relations and rural power.
  • Landownership and tenure: Land reforms sought to abolish intermediaries, regulate
  • tenancy and redistribute surplus land. Their effects varied across regions. Unequal
  • ownership, insecure tenancy and fragmentation remain significant features of agrarian
  • society.
  • Technology and production: Irrigation, improved seeds, fertilisers and mechanisation
  • increased agricultural productivity in many areas. The Green Revolution particularly
  • benefited regions and cultivators with access to land, water and capital, contributing to
  • uneven development.
  • Commercialisation: Cultivation increasingly responds to markets through cash crops
  • purchased inputs, credit and commercial supply chains. This creates opportunities but also
  • exposes cultivators to fluctuating prices, rising costs and indebtedness.
  • Labour relations: Hereditary service relationships and personal dependence have weakened
  • in many areas. Wage labour, seasonal migration and mechanisation have altered agricultural
  • employment, although caste and gender inequalities persist.
  • Class and power relations: Changes in land, credit and production have strengthened some
  • prosperous cultivators and rural entrepreneurs. Small farmers and landless workers often
  • face greater insecurity.
  • Diversification and migration: Rural households increasingly combine farming with
  • construction work, services, small businesses and migration.
  • Gender and ecology: Women undertake substantial agricultural work but often lack
  • ownership and decision-making power. Water scarcity, soil degradation and climate
  • variability also shape agrarian livelihoods.
  • Agrarian change is therefore an uneven transformation of rural production, inequality and
  • power.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; explained dimensions — 6; conclusion/example — 1.
  • 14(b). Analyse Ghurye’s treatment of tribes and integration, including criticisms of his
  • assimilationist approach.
  • G. S. Ghurye understood many Indian tribal communities through their historical interaction
  • with the wider Hindu social order. He challenged the idea that tribes were entirely isolated
  • societies.
  • Tribe–caste connections: Ghurye emphasised cultural contact and similarities between tribal
  • populations and surrounding Hindu communities. He described many tribes as “backward
  • Hindus,” reflecting his interpretation that they had varying degrees of incorporation into
  • Hindu society.
  • Opposition to isolation: He opposed policies that would preserve tribal communities in
  • isolation. He favoured their participation in wider economic, educational and political life.
  • Assimilation: His approach generally supported incorporation into the wider Hindu social
  • order and national society. Education, communication and economic development were
  • important means of overcoming marginalisation.
  • Criticisms
  •  Cultural diversity: The category “backward Hindus” can obscure the distinct
  • religions, languages, institutions and identities of tribal communities.
  •  Hindu-centred interpretation: It treats incorporation into Hindu society as the
  • expected direction of change.
  •  Power and exploitation: Cultural incorporation does not necessarily remove
  • dispossession, indebtedness or exploitation.
  •  Autonomy and consent: Assimilation may neglect communities’ rights to determine
  • their own futures.
  •  Cultural loss: Incorporation can undermine indigenous knowledge and collective
  • institutions.
  • Ghurye’s contribution lies in highlighting historical connections between tribes and wider
  • society. However, an adequate approach to integration must combine equal opportunities
  • with cultural recognition, land rights and self-determination.
  • Suggested marking: Ghurye’s approach — 4; criticisms — 3; assessment — 1.
  • 15(a). Discuss discrimination, endogamy and unequal resources as contemporary
  • challenges related to caste.
  • Caste continues to shape opportunities and relationships despite substantial changes in
  • education, employment and public life.
  • Discrimination: Caste discrimination can occur in schools, workplaces, housing and public
  • spaces. It includes exclusion, humiliation, prejudiced judgments and unequal treatment.
  • Some forms are overt, while others operate through informal practices and networks.
  • Example: A qualified person may encounter housing exclusion because of their caste
  • identity.
  • Endogamy: Marriage within one’s caste remains a major mechanism of caste continuity.
  • Families may use caste-based networks and matrimonial preferences to regulate partner
  • selection. Opposition to inter-caste marriage can range from emotional pressure to violence.
  • Endogamy preserves caste boundaries by linking marriage with family status, inheritance
  • and community membership.
  • Unequal resources: Historical differences in landownership, education, assets and
  • occupational opportunities continue to influence present outcomes. Families with
  • substantial resources can provide better schooling, financial support and access to influential
  • networks. Disadvantaged households may face insecure work and limited opportunities for
  • accumulation.
  • Interconnection: Discrimination restricts opportunities, resource inequalities reduce
  • bargaining power, and endogamy helps transmit these advantages and disadvantages across
  • generations.
  • Addressing caste therefore requires both protection against exclusion and measures that
  • expand access to education, resources, dignified employment and freedom of marriage.
  • Suggested marking: Introduction — 1; three challenges — 6; conclusion — 1.
  • 15(b). Analyse why modern caste politics is not simply the survival of traditional politics.
  • Modern caste politics involves the transformation of caste identities through elections
  • democratic institutions, political parties and struggles over resources.
  • From inherited authority to electoral mobilisation: Traditional caste authority was closely
  • associated with hereditary status and local dominance. Electoral politics requires leaders to
  • mobilise voters and negotiate support.
  • Political participation of subordinated groups: Dalit, backward-caste and other movements
  • have challenged established hierarchies. Their mobilisation expresses demands for dignity
  • representation and redistribution.
  • New caste organisations: Caste associations may organise education, welfare, employment
  • support and political campaigns. These organisations use modern institutional forms and
  • communication technologies.
  • Coalition-building: Electoral success often requires alliances across castes. Political blocs are
  • constructed through negotiation rather than determined entirely by ritual hierarchy.
  • State resources and policy: Representation, reservations, welfare and access to public
  • institutions have become major political concerns. Caste thus becomes a basis for claims
  • upon the modern state.
  • Changing leadership: Education, organisational ability and political connections can create
  • leaders whose influence does not rest solely on traditional rank.
  • Continuing contradictions: Caste mobilisation can democratise power, but it can also
  • promote exclusion, elite capture and conflict.
  • Modern caste politics therefore combines inherited identities with new institutions and
  • aspirations. It may reproduce inequality, but it can also provide a means of challenging it.
  • Suggested marking: Central argument — 1; analysis — 6; balanced conclusion — 1.
  • 16(a). Examine changing inter-caste relations in work, politics and everyday interaction.
  • Inter-caste relations have changed through education, migration, democratic participation
  • economic development and anti-caste struggles. These changes vary across regions and
  • social settings.
  • Work: Hereditary links between caste and occupation have weakened in many sectors.
  • People from different castes work together in offices, factories, educational institutions and
  • service industries. However, caste networks still influence recruitment and advancement
  • while stigmatised work remains disproportionately associated with particular communities.
  • Politics: Electoral democracy has expanded participation and enabled historically
  • disadvantaged groups to challenge dominant castes. Political parties build inter-caste
  • alliances and negotiate competing demands. At the same time, caste competition can
  • generate polarisation and conflict.
  • Everyday interaction: Shared schools, transport, markets and workplaces have increased
  • contact across caste boundaries. Restrictions on commensality and physical interaction have
  • weakened in many settings.
  • Continuing boundaries: Greater interaction does not always produce intimate social
  • acceptance. Marriage remains strongly regulated by caste, and exclusion can persist in
  • housing, neighbourhood relations and access to common resources.
  • Uneven change: Urban anonymity and occupational diversity may weaken some controls
  • while local dependence and unequal landownership can sustain them elsewhere. Caste
  • discrimination also exists in cities.
  • Inter-caste relations thus show expanding cooperation alongside continuing hierarchy and
  • contested boundaries.
  • Suggested marking: Introduction — 1; work, politics and everyday interaction — 6; synthesis
  • — 1.
  • 16(b). Discuss the meaning and major dimensions of women’s empowerment.
  • Women’s empowerment is the process through which women gain resources, agency and
  • the ability to make meaningful decisions about their lives. It also involves transforming
  • institutions that sustain gender inequality.
  • Educational empowerment: Access to education, skills and digital literacy improves
  • knowledge, confidence and opportunities.
  • Economic empowerment: Access to decent employment, fair earnings, property, credit and
  • control over income strengthens independence and bargaining power.
  • Political empowerment: Voting, representation, leadership and participation in public
  • decisions enable women to influence policies and institutions.
  • Social empowerment: Freedom from restrictive norms, violence and discrimination
  • supports mobility, dignity and participation in community life.
  • Legal empowerment: Awareness of rights and effective access to justice help women
  • challenge unequal treatment and secure entitlements.
  • Health and bodily autonomy: Access to healthcare and the ability to make informed
  • decisions about marriage, sexuality and reproduction are essential.
  • Psychological empowerment: Self-confidence and recognition of one’s capacity to act help
  • women express preferences and challenge domination.
  • Example: A self-help group may offer savings and credit while also enabling collective action
  • and leadership.
  • Empowerment requires actual control and choice. Employment or formal representation
  • alone may have limited effects if others continue to control women’s decisions.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 2; explained dimensions — 5; example/conclusion — 1.
  • 17(a). Explain the structure and key characteristics of the Indian village community.
  • The Indian village community is a rural settlement whose members are connected through
  • residence, livelihoods, kinship, institutions and everyday interaction. Villages differ
  • considerably across regions.
  • Agrarian foundation: Agriculture and related activities have historically shaped village
  • livelihoods, social relations and seasonal routines.
  • Caste differentiation: Many villages contain several caste groups, sometimes living in distinct
  • neighbourhoods. Caste has influenced status, occupation and access to resources.
  • Class inequality: Differences between landowners, tenants, small cultivators and landless
  • workers create unequal economic positions.
  • Family and kinship: Families, lineages and marriage networks organise inheritance, support
  • and social obligations.
  • Local power: Landownership, caste position, wealth and political connections influence
  • leadership. Panchayats provide formal institutions of local governance.
  • Religious and cultural life: Festivals, religious institutions and local traditions can generate
  • shared participation, although participation may also reflect exclusion and hierarchy.
  • Cooperation and conflict: Villagers may cooperate in cultivation, ceremonies and local
  • development while also competing over land, wages, water and political authority.
  • External connections: Villages are linked to towns, markets, migration networks
  • government agencies and digital communication.
  • The village should therefore be understood as a changing and internally differentiated
  • community, rather than a uniformly harmonious or self-sufficient unit.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; structure and characteristics — 6; critical observation —
